What I like a lot less are Dishonest Fake Expressions, where the person is acting and trying to present the smile as if it is real, and does not want you to know it is fake.

Know a guy who owns a truck. Then you can move things, or all the things. The cost is buying the pizza afterwards, plus helping out when it is your turn to help. The system works, and it makes everyone richer in a real sense and builds community, but lowers measured GDP. A lot of the story of vibecession and related topics, where economists say you are richer and poor people insist they are instead poorer, is explained by this.

The account here, Nobunaga, has many similarly good stories about a particular American set of norms around community cooperation, reputation, honesty and virtuous norms. I do not take them to be literally true, but this is not important. They are fables in support of norms. Those that have such norms will vastly overperform measured GDP, and people will be happier. Those that lack such norms will underperform measured GDP, and people will be less happy.

The norms are not always efficient, and can be taken too far. The electrician should not be impossible to reach. When you are in higher demand you should charge more, and so on. Growth and productivity rates suffer. I am generally a fan of more capitalism. But something important and valuable is being lost.

If there is going to be an Unexpected Hanging some day this week, what are your options?

Eliezer Yudkowsky: Apply Ultrafinite Recursion:
– The teacher reasons that they cannot give the test on Friday, or students will know.
– The teacher realizes that students may realize the teacher realizes this, ruling out Thursday.
– Humans recurse at most 3 levels, so Mon/Tue/Weds all possible.

Note this assumes a teacher operating at actual max recursion, modeling students modeling teacher modeling students. Less smart teachers, or teachers who model their students as dumb, may give test Thursday.

You may observe that to solve this problem I had to model the teacher modeling the students modeling the teacher modeling the students. I can do this because secretly at WIS 22 the max level goes up to 4.

Robert Garritty: But each iteration of this reasoning starts the recursion back at 0. If Mon/Tuesday/Wednesday are all possible, then Wednesday’s not possible, and so on. This doesn’t resolve the paradox.

Eliezer Yudkowsky: Nope, the teacher could test you on Wednesday and it would be a surprise to you (uncertain) because given that the teacher has already waited until Wednesday, you don’t know whether the teacher is smart enough, or thinks you’re smart enough, that they wouldn’t test on Thursday.

Which in turn, I argue, means you can also test on Friday, because on Friday you will think it would not be a surprise so therefore they can’t give the test, which means it will be a surprise.

Astrology is a hell of a placebo, with people who read horoscopes exhibiting 0.2 standard deviations of self-reported personality movement towards their sign, whereas the effect size for others is exactly zero.

Good News, Everyone

If you want to ensure you can cancel your subscriptions, credit cards do offer some options. You can use X1, Rho or privacy.com to spin up a new card for each subscription. You can use Mercury, which allows you to easily block merchants. And so on. I presume AI will soon be able to handle this for you rather easily either way.

The Apple Vision Pro is a dud with consumers. They did not deliver the killer apps, interface and linked capabilities to justify the price point, charging issues and weight. But technically it is an excellent product, such as improving performance in endoscopic lacrimal surgery while being under 1% of the cost of an endoscopic display tower. The linked study has low sample size, so treat with caution.

The NFL press box food offerings, ranked. I appreciated this, I eat very differently but we are kindred spirits in the ways that count. Amazing how many teams are bad at it.

Ordinary Abundance. Many found this highly moving.

For Your Entertainment

Coyote vs. Acme is the third 5-star movie of 2026, matching 2024 and 2025 combined. Recommended for literal everyone of all ages.

I tried an experiment with turning Letterboxd’s top algorithmic picks for me into a Manifold market. It did not go great. Almost no strong opinions were expressed, and the top pick, The Grand Budapest Hotel, was a bitter disappointment. Perhaps my readers can make better picks. You can add new suggestions to the market, as well.

I agree with Tyler Cowen that it does seem like movies peaked in specifically 1999, as per the speech in The Matrix about that being the pinnacle of your civilization. Then movies got worse in key ways, including too many franchises wasting top budgets and talent. Now movies are getting better again. 2026 has been fantastic.

What about Game of Thrones? We have two narratives fighting to this day, between ‘Season 8 fell off a cliff’ and ‘seasons 5-7 also kind of sucked.’

Javier Cañavate #HouseOfTheDragon: It hurts to see how season 8 breaks the vibe

The Late Knight Show: Do not fall for the “Sh0w wAs Go0d unT1l seas0n 8” propaganda

To the people are lashing out at this:

This doesn’t mean that the show was Bas since season 1. GOT is fucking excellent from seasons 1 to 4. There’s merit to season 5

Season 6 sucks. Seasons 7 and 8 are a fucking travesty. I ain’t hearing you out.

Memory is blurry by now, but I think the truth is in between. Things clearly were best in the first 4 seasons, top level television. The momentum and some great moments carried us through 5, 6 and largely even 7, and fans kept voting high because they wanted it to be great and the characters and scenes were still often individually great. Then in season 8 it became impossible to pretend.

My general thesis continues to be that it is better for shows to overstay their welcomes, and to sacrifice quality on the margin for quantity. It doesn’t have to get this bad, but unless the story has a clear fixed length, keep it going. Often the later parts that aren’t strictly ‘as good’ are still very good in their own way, and occasionally they age well once you’re over the initial disappointment.

Are you ready for Avengers: Doomsday? Collect them all.

Marvel Updates: Disney+ has released a list of essential projects to watch before ‘AVENGERS: DOOMSDAY’:

• X-Men
• X2
• Captain America: The First Avenger
• The Avengers
• Avengers: Infinity War
• Avengers: Endgame
• Loki
• Shang-Chi and The Legend of The Ten Rings
• Spider-Man: No Way Home
• Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness
• Black Panther: Wakanda Forever
• Deadpool & Wolverine
• Captain America: Brave New World
• Thunderbolts*
• The Fantastic Four: First Steps

That is asking a lot. I am two movies short. But they’re likely a tough two movies, especially Brave New World.

The state of DVDs, I still find this beautiful even though I have abandoned all use of physical media:

Employee #84 : Bought 488 DVDs from an estate sale today for $30. I guess I’m starting a flea market in my front yard.

We need movie theaters that show a wider variety of movies, and show things for longer.

Mike Drucker: Bring back cheap second run movie theaters. I don’t give a shit if it’s on streaming already. Charge $5 for the odyssey or spider-man in December and people would go just to kill time. Don’t ask me if it’s economically feasible became I don’t fucking know.

Zack Stentz: Each major studio used to have a guy whose whole job it was to squeeze the last couple million out of every theatrical release, and he was usually on a first name basis with the manager of every dollar theater in America.
It was a better time.

I have seen enough empty theaters to know that it would be viable. The opportunity cost of off-peak showings is very low. I also would love a low-cost all-theater rental option for off-peak times.

Or how about letting an individual choose the movie for some modest marginal cost? If on average you sell 5 tickets, and I am willing to buy 5 tickets a week in advance and want to put on Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, do it and see if anyone else comes.

What has been working great is the Anniversary editions of older films. I am increasingly seeing movies from 20 or 30 years ago having brief runs at AMC, and it is glorious, I need to make it more of a priority to attend.

The craziest part is that they are often ‘excluded from A-list,’ which means they charge you like $20 instead of $0, and yet they sell a lot of tickets. This clearly means there aren’t enough such offerings, and they don’t hold them open long enough.

The addiction economy:

Henry Shevlin: One of these things is not like the others.

Brad Wilcox: We have a generation of young men trapped in the “addiction economy”—and the numbers are staggering:

1-in-8 use porn, gamble & game daily
Almost 1-in-4 gamble daily
1-in-4+ use porn daily

I continue to be a big fan of video games, in moderation or even somewhat more than moderation, provided they are ‘good’ games. None of the three things here are inherently bad. The problem is lack of moderation, or getting trapped in bad versions. The version on your phone will usually be the bad version of all three.

I did a Twitter poll (now lost to time) where I asked which of these three things was not like the others, and got defenders of all three.

Correct toon logic: Sonic is faster than the Road Runner (probably), but if Sonic tried to catch the Roadrunner he could definitely fail and probably blow himself up.

Terminator 2 is a great move on entertainment alone, Jeffrey Ladish finally watched it and asks about how accurate it is on the AI front once you ignore the time travel and the Terminators. The answer is better than you would think, especially the emphasis that the dangerous thing was the computer that went into recursive self-improvement rather than the robots.

The big ‘real’ issue is that Skynet learns and gains power absurdly fast at first, and then stalls out at exactly the level where it can somehow be defeated by a John Connor and a ragtag group of survivors, because otherwise the time loop would not close and also we do not have a movie or franchise. This is the typical Hollywood ‘intelligence stops doing anything, and also the AI’s efforts stop scaling, at exactly the point where the humans can still barely win’ which exists for reasons that should be obvious, both in Hollywood and also in the real debates over AI. People like humans winning, and people like telling human stories.

Please Review This Podcast

Many solid choices by Dean Ball. For me this splits into ‘things that I can confirm are very good’ and ‘things I have not listened to and thus it is hard to say but they have good company.’

I am especially a fan, from this list, of Cognitive Revolution, Conversations with Tyler, Odd Lots, Dwarkesh Podcast, Money Stuff and Complex Systems. Dwarkesh suffers from being ‘too good’ so I end up often reading transcripts instead. I sometimes listen to Lex Fridman and 80,000 Hours, as well as AXRP, but long pod is long and I choose topics.

Dean W. Ball: i doubt anyone cares but here are my most listened to podcasts so far this year. many of the hosts of these shows follow me and you should know I think you’re awesome, even if we have never met or spoken.

Anastasia Gamick: Dean, where does this free time come from??

Dean W. Ball: I don’t sleep very much

At some point I will write about at least some of my favorite podcasts. Two not here that I very much enjoy are Wait Wait, Don’t Tell Me and Serious Trouble, and I at least sometimes listen to EconTalk, Clearer Thinking, Win-Win and Plain English.

There are also some that fall into a different category of gaming and entertainment. It can’t all be work stuff. My favorite Magic podcast is All Tings Considered, but that is constrained by my ‘I do not know what the new cards do’ problem.

Gamers Gonna Game Game Game Game Game

You can now report players on Magic the Gathering: Arena. There are five complaints: Inactivity, Hate Speech, Inappropriate Username, Verbal Abuse and Spamming.

Three of these seem silly given the lack of communication channels. But it is very good to be able to report players for Inactivity, also known as stalling, which players do either because they are mad at you, because they can or in the hopes that you will give up or accidentally time out.

Andrea Mengucci proposes ways to help bring back competitive Magic, including more focus on Pauper as a cheap format. I’m ‘out of the game’ in all senses, so it’s hard for me to evaluate the current situation, but the obvious thing is that Magic is huge yet they give you very little to strive for. Every reasonable solution starts with running real tournaments, with strong prizes, and ways to accumulate points, qualify for things and earn money, pride and titles, including room for some people to be Pros off of results rather than streaming. Wizards is not doing this because they don’t care, not because they do not know how. I guess they do not like money.

I Was Promised Flying Self-Driving Cars

Human Progress: Swiss Re, one of the world’s leading reinsurers, found that Waymo’s autonomous vehicles generated 88% fewer property damage claims and 92% fewer bodily injury claims than human-driven vehicles.

On September 1, Waymo opened service in Denver, San Diego and Tampa.

Waymo once again expands its approved service area in Greater San Francisco as well as Los Angeles. Most of this region will be waiting for a while, but this means Waymo will have no trouble finding good uses its cars for a while no matter what happens elsewhere.

I continue to eagerly await Waymo coming to East Bay, given that is where I usually visit. Alas, the odds look bad, and say a majority of the time this won’t happen even in 2027. Complaints are the prices remain too high, which is another way of saying demand exceeds supply.

Tesla asks for permits for 5,000 robotaxis in Las Vegas, was initially given 10 but has now been approved for the full 5,000. Waymo and Uber each got 1,000.

There are some things self-driving cars probably won’t ever do for you.

Nate Silver: Robotaxis are very cool but there’s probably going to be a weird equilibrium where human drivers have some competitive advantage because they’re less strict about following speed limits and traffic laws.

Mike Solana: waymo already increased aggression. down in LA, especially, drivers wouldn’t let them out of four-way stops. you can feel the difference on the roads, now, even as a pedestrian. they’re not the docile creatures they were last year.

Misha: Waymo will never truly replace human cab drivers until I can flag one down, jump in and shout “Follow that car! Step on it!”

Waymo gets into an accident that makes the news. As one would expect, it is minor contact and entirely not the Waymo’s fault.

Not to be outdone, Waymo ‘nearly ran over’ a two-year old, said many. This is the framing people go with for ‘actual nothing happened and it was not close.’

SFist: A father in Noe Valley says a Waymo robotaxi stopped within 13 feet of his two-year-old daughter when she fell in the crosswalk, nearly running her over, but Waymo claims the car wouldn’t have hit her.

Alex Immerman: “Waymo nearly ran over a 2-year-old” is an irresponsible framing. The Waymo stopped 13 feet away. Two king size mattresses placed end-to-end fit between. If my kid fell in a crosswalk, I’d be terrified. I’d also be grateful the approaching car was a Waymo.

Divia Eden : I think cars with superhuman breaking are part of what might make the world way safer for kids to roam, and they can’t arrive soon enough IMO!

‘I literally don’t know what you want from me’ very much applies here. The Waymo did exactly what you would want it to do, complete with displaying ‘pedestrian yield,’ and the complaint seems to be that the father was worried that it might not do that?

Yes, I very much worry that one accident will ruin everything. Eventually there will be one accident.

Government Working

I will never understand the idea that it is good and right to arrest people for making edgy jokes in a private WhatsApp group, without anyone in the group even minding, as happens in the UK. How does anyone describe this as anything but utter insanity?

Flock cameras plus AI is coming, while Flock demos things like ‘how to monitor a protest in real time.’ Have we considered not allowing the creation of a dystopian surveillance network for the government or others to hook up to their AIs?

Mamdani (Again) Fails Economics Forever

I will keep harping on the Mamdani NYC city-run grocery store fiasco, mainly because it is funny.

Dan Rivoli: Lead official for Mayor Mamdani’s NYC Groceries tells me city may give grants to local grocers fearing competition from city-run stores

“policies and programs, grants, incentives that can come alongside these grocery stores to support other local independent businesses”

Dan Rivoli: Clean up, aisle 5. Spokesman for @NYCEDC , which oversees NYC Groceries for Mayor Mamdani, sent me a statement today saying:

“We are not currently considering any grant programs” for grocers competing with city stores, but rather tax abatements and zoning benefits

Catherine Rampell: Hear me out. What if instead of selling food below cost to all comers at taxpayer expense, and then using more taxpayer dollars to subsidize private companies that can’t compete with those prices, we had a program that targeted nutritional assistance just to the people who needed it, as a supplement? We could call it, I don’t know, supplemental nutritional assistance

To those who think 115th & Park is a “food desert”: I have an Aldi, Costco, Shop Fair, Whole Foods, Foodtown, CTown, Food Bazaar, and Target to sell you

Here is 115th & Park, where the new store presumably will go:

Dan Rivoli: This is the second time a key part of NYC Groceries had to be walked back. First was when an official said there would be a “library card-esque” system to prevent resale. After reasonable inference that ID would be required, mayor himself had to say no ID would be required

They keep changing their story because there are zero ways to implement the thing they want that do not end in disaster.

Variously Effective Altruism

Remember what the benchmark is, in two parts.

Part 1: The super rich do things like pay a specialty agency $100,000 per year with a $1 million spending minimum above that, and then spend absurd amounts of money on whims and momentary thrills, and most of all on getting exactly the things they want whenever they want them, and yes they are often jaded. Olivia Ferney, a travel specialist they hire, confirms, as we learn in How To Make A Killing, that you might want to think this means they are miserable, but actually the super rich are happy with the results, thank you very much.

I totally get it, especially the part where you have a person you can call that makes happen whatever you want to happen. Must be nice. But I’d feel sick about it, and not only because I could have given the money away. I sometimes wonder how many extra zeroes I’d need on my net worth before I’d feel entitled to start acting like this. At least two, but less than five.

Part 2:

Yonan: Seth Rogen says his financial fear is dying with $10 million in the bank that he could have spent while he was alive.

“I’m afraid I’m going to die with too much money. I don’t have children, and I’m afraid I’m going to die and be like, I could have had a place at the beach”

“I don’t want to die with like $10,000,000 in the bank that I could have spent doing fun, alive things”

“A jet to Paris on a whim? Yeah, exactly. I could have been jetting. I could have been jetting this whole time”

This, on the other hand, feels completely insane, even if you have Too Much Money. Which Seth Rogen clearly does. Costs are not benefits, and the point of having money is partly to spend it but also to have the peace of mind that it is there when you need it. The value of that extra $10 million spent while rich is a tiny fraction of how much you would miss it if you lived longer than you expect while in any danger of being poor.

Dying with nothing in the bank, or close to nothing, is a huge disaster, far worse for Seth Rogan than dying with $10 million.

That’s even if you discount that you could use the money to actually help people.

So, yeah, I criticize it a lot, but maybe this whole ‘effective altruism’ thing is actually pretty good.

How Sarah Constantin thinks about evaluating grant applications, here condensed with a slight Zvi slant to the explanations, as we think highly similarly here. I endorse basically all of this.

  1. It’s the donor’s money, spend it on what the donor cares about.
  2. Importance, neglectedness, tractability.
  3. Yay community infrastructure, especially for the donor’s community.
  4. Yay niche topics, that matter to the donor.
  5. Yay ‘technical’ work, involving rare unfakeable skill, like making a thing.
  6. Yay straightforward public information resources.
  7. Yay ‘cool shit’ even if there isn’t an obvious payoff beyond being cool.
  8. Two cheers for meta. Keep a mix of meta and object level.
  9. Gumption counts. If the person wants to do it, there is a reason.
  10. Yay personal relationships. Use your local knowledge, including of people.
  11. Check ideological orientation, in case it interacts with the project.
  12. Filter slop aggressively. Do not waste our time.
  13. Yay outcomes that are concrete and legible, not always but it helps.
  14. Invest rather than donate where that would make sense.

If Hell does not exist, then we do not need to create it. We already have New Jersey.

A highly underrated charity strategy is Give Effective People Money, especially retroactive funding for things you loved, with no strings attached. Also speed kills.

Chris Lakin: if you’re capital looking for philanthropic stuff to fund… consider retroactively funding work that already happened that you loved. give those people no-strings funds to do more whimsical stuff (or do whatever they want) without requiring them to waste time on applications AND you build reputation for yourself as the serious funder to be connected to. (there are too many funders who say they’re “interested” in funding xyz, but never actually do anything, so you could build a great reputation really quick)

Charles: I did this once (gave somebody with a good track record ~£30k to buy out their time so they could focus on whatever they thought most valuable vs whatever paid at the time) but Jan Tallinn then gave them like 10x that a few months later (not due to anything that happened in between I think) so the counterfactual impact was pretty low.

Chris Lakin: Wdym seems like you got them started multiple months earlier? That’s huge

Charles: Nah the lag on the money arriving due to EA regrantor lag meant I don’t think they actually had the money yet

Moral intuitions very different from my own, remember that this was asking ‘what do others do’ not ‘what should people do’:

Robin Hanson: According to poll, relative strength of moral guides others use:

Robin was as usual Robin Hansoning, as he described reason as ‘argued for by our impressive thinkers’ rather than ‘what the person thinks is right, based on their own reason.’ As you would expect, Robin then argues hard against using your conscience.

A very clear case for Effective Altruism, especially from Patrick McKenzie:

Kelsey Piper: I’m an effective altruist because 1) I care a lot about how I can best use my money and time to achieve my goals in the world, and EAs wrote a lot of the stuff I found useful on that topic and 2) EA told me in the 2010s to worry about AI and pandemics, and they were right.

Patrick McKenzie: I wouldn’t self-identify as an EA, and if one hypothetically read the Day 6 Vaccinate CA memo, one would find language in it which resonated with EAs and one would find language in it which resonated with Tolkien.

If I can be permitted to make personal empirical observations:

100% of funders who have expressed regret they did not fund VaccinateCA themselves self-identify as EA.

100% of funders who have contacted me post VaccinateCA offering to backfill money I personally donated the organization self-identify as EA.

Given base rates among college-educated Americans, EAs were _wildly_ overrepresented among early volunteers and coordinators. Even adjusting for the tech industry lineage/seed set/theory of change I think this remains true.

People who are reasonably read as barometers of community opinion tell me that VaccinateCA is wildly impressive evidence of efficacy in their community, with respect to EAs.

No person in the California government or public health field has ever said this to me directly.

(I will report, for completeness’ sake, that I have been told through an intermediary that the _writeup_ of VaccinateCA was considered above-replacement-rate for a postmortem by a senior official in public health. I offered a meeting. EAs have taken meetings w/ me.)

The Lighter Side

Sometimes I have sympathy for people who lose money but if you bought Hunter Biden’s $LAPTOP right before it crashed 98% within an hour of its launch then I do not really know what you were expecting.

Spotted on Letterboxd about La La Land, some people are a tough crowd:

Clayton Petty: Louvre. Immediately.

In case anyone was wondering, yes, I will also always think like this.

Proof by counterexample:

Cheat, cheat, cheat, cheat, cheat. IYKYK, if not see here.

content:
Lately I've been playing classic World of Warcraft to get a feel for it and see if I like it before I try and go head-first into WoW Forever fairly blind with some friends. People have told me that World of Warcraft is good, but I haven't personally played it (or really any MMO outside of Final Fantasy 14). I've wanted to see for myself, so I dug in.

I've been leveling an undead warlock and recently I've gotten my way to The Barrens. My goal was to kill some planestriders and collect their beaks as proof of my kills so that the population can get back under control or whatever. I wandered around and found another player also on that quest and waved to them. He was a gnome warlock named Borton and waved at me when I walked over. I waved back and invited him to a party. We walked around the area and started spreading our aggro to farm the planestriders and grab their drops. After a few kills he stopped for a second and said "this is why we play".

I was taken a bit aback by this. It felt out of nowhere but also felt like one of the more human encounters I've had with people in a video game in a long time. One of the great parts about MMOs is that you end up having a lot of these itinerant bits of community like this. You both get a quest from an NPC asking you to go and farm some drops and then this sends you all out into the world to naturally do it together. These conversations and liminal bits of community end up adding up into the greater experiences and really giving you the flavour of the game's vibe. You do it together for the fun of the game.

After a while we finished our farming, got all the planestrider beaks, commiserated about the drop tables, and decided to just sit down on a nearby hill and take a screenshot because it just felt right.

This has really gotten me thinking about what I really want to get out of games and why I play them. I think I've been doing it wrong.

The endless treadmill of “dead content”

At some level the “high end” content of online games like Final Fantasy 14 or Retail World of Warcraft looks endless. There’s intricate dances of choreography as you and your friends puzzle your way through each boss mechanic towards victory. Hell, games like Final Fantasy 14 have their fights defined by the little call->response pairs as the boss telegraphs things and you react to it in concert. Not to mention the feeling of utter serotonin that comes from figuring it out and winning.

One of the main problems with this is that the “high end” raids in this game tend to be a mile wide in theory but practically an inch deep. Don’t get me wrong, even as far back as a decade ago there’s still encounters that are actually hard (eg: XIV’s ultimate raids, I'm personally at Quickmarch Trio in UCOB if you have the right brainworms to know what that means), but as the fights get older there’s a sharp dropoff in the number of people that actually want to run them. This ends up with entire subsystems of the game (Deep Dungeons, Bozja before Shadowbringers went into the free trial, etc) becoming “dead content” because if you queue for them, nobody shows up. If you put up an entry for them in Party Finder, nobody will join you unless you set aside time to wait for hours. You end up with modes where you're encouraged to do it in a group being bereft of people so you're "forced" to figure it out on your own.

As a result everyone is funneled into the high end and trying to min-max it as much as possible to squeeze all the game they can out as fast as they can before “everyone else” gets what they want out of it and moves on. The world becomes a theme park where only the newest rides have the most people there and getting a group for anything else becomes a slog in party finder or needing you to seek out people that focus on that thing and nothing else.

This also means that if you’re “slow” or have to take a break during the small sliver when content is “current”, you’re going to be stuck "behind" on it for a long time without significant effort to find a way around it. It really makes you wonder what the point of it all is if you can’t find anyone to do it. Worse, when you're trying to find a group to do it regularly (a "static" group), they look at how you did on previous raid tiers as a way to vet if you're a "shitter" or not.

The records of your ultimate achievements of an entire raid tier, or the relic weapons for an entire expansion just end up becoming things you can do if you want that give you a shiny skin for your weapons to coordinate with an outfit that looks better. Maybe in edge cases those stats will be better for complicated maths reasons. All that effort you put into them is just ultimately "wasted" when the next ride comes out, all the stats get reset, and everyone moves on to wait in line for the next thing. All of your gear you spent weeks grinding for is reduced to sticks that increase the statistics correlated to aspects of your character that make the funny numbers go up so you can kill the boss faster to move on to the next thing.

Maybe this is just something endemic to the theme park design philosophy where you’re given a goal by the developers and a series of actions that really boil down to TODO items that are the barrier from you and that thing you actually want (do these quests, fight these normal raid bosses, beat the savage versions of those bosses, beat the ultimate boss, get the shiny weapons, and finally look cool afk-ing in Limsa Lominsa). Maybe this is why people end up seeing things like the overworld as the barrier to the rides instead of an integral part of the experience. Maybe this is the pressure that makes people want to have flying mounts or other ways to "skip the grind".

A meditation on Death Stranding

I haven't really touched Death Stranding since I did my review on it way back in 2019. It's always had a special place in my heart though, it's kind of a touching experience even though it's incredibly isolating at the same time. This game has two main characters: Sam "Porter" Bridges and the game world. The overworld's system of traversal is the protagonist as much as the actual protagonist is.

Honestly I think one of the best features of Death Stranding is the camera mode. At any point you can hit a button (on the Steam Controller it's one of the back buttons by default) and the action stops so you can position the camera and just soak in the scenery. If you've never played Death Stranding before, I highly suggest you stop reading this post right now and buy it on whatever platform you buy games on. Worst case you can experience it on the iPhone as Hideo Kojima surely intended.



[image or embed]

— Xe (

@xeiaso.net

)

September 20, 2026 at 12:02 PM

Cadey

If you actually do this on an iPhone, please do it with a controller. The touch controls are kinda awful.

As you progress your way delivering packages to save America, every so often the camera will pull back, the game actions will become muted, and the normally contemplative and silent experience will suddenly be augmented by soft music.

It turns this process of progression into a serene bit of negative space in a way that makes you really stop and think about the experience, the dramatis personae, and the kind of story that's trying to be conveyed. The world itself turns into this sense of wanderlust that makes you mentally pause and just process things.

I don't really know if I'm doing this justice, in the moment it's an almost spiritual kind of connection between you and the overworld mediated by the soft sounds of Silent Poets' Asylum For The Feeling or Low Roar's Don't Be So Serious. The game makes you feel so small yet so connected to the world around you and there's just this overwhelming sense of equanimity.

Just take a moment to watch the Don't Be So Serious video with Death Stranding gameplay underlaid. That's a snapshot of how the game literally plays out. It's these liminal bits of wanderlust combined with a story that only Kojima or Yoko Taro could come up with.

I miss the feeling of exploring

This kind of overwhelming emotion is the kind of thing that made me fall in love with gaming back in the days when the most complicated games I'd play would be Banjo Kazooie, Super Mario 64, Super Mario Sunshine, Pikmin 2, Sonic Adventure 2, and other games of that vintage. At some level I kind of long for not knowing what's beyond the next hill and being forced to figure it out by just going there to find out.

Hell, I also get this sense of romance in Breath of the Wild or Tears of the Kingdom when I just turn off all the UI elements and wander around wherever the wind takes me.

Breath of the Wild is one of those games where you can just wander around the overworld for ages and still find new things. Combine it with flying and you just feel things as you go from hither to thither. Even with fast travel you still have to go there yourself. You have to climb every mountain. You have to cross the vast expanse of the desert. You have to figure out how to get a boat to the island with some awesome gear. And even months or years after you capture screenshots/video of the adventure, looking at them takes you back there and you just feel it again.

You have the power and you have to pick what you do with it. There is no wrong way to do it. Want to fly over Gerudo Town after sunset knowing well and good that the moment you land you're gonna get kicked out of it for being a guy? Hell yeah, you can just DO IT.

This is making me think, fuck, am I actually getting what I want out of my time? In my race to min-max my way through "current" things so I don't get "behind" have I just lost that sense of wanderlust from the experience? I miss that feeling of just exploring the world for what it is and letting myself get there the long way.

Have I been skipping over the real "good part" in my effort to be efficient in getting to what I thought the "good part" really was?

Have I just been playing games the wrong way?

This is why we play

I think I've been playing the games I'm immersing myself in incorrectly and I want to change that. I want to lose myself in the fantasy worlds. I want to let myself see the sights, hear the sounds, feel the breeze on my back, go fishing at what feels like the little corner of civilization just at the edge of the universe, and just let that sense of overwhelming wanderlust come back into my life.

This is why we play, we play to let the fantasies of these fantasy worlds take charge and show you something that you didn't think you needed in your life yet you're all the richer for it. As World of Warcraft Forever comes out in November and Final Fantasy 14's Evercold expansion comes out next year, I'm going to just let those worlds enrapture me in their designs and lose myself to the wanderlust. I'll let The Fourth take me where it does and that's okay.

It's absurd that the root of this revelation was a bot in a single-player MMO on my homelab picking a random chat message out of a list of dozens randomly triggered by a random overworld mob dying.

Yeah, I forgot to mention, this all was caused by an experiment in playing with bots to teach me what it means to have a community. I was gonna lead this post with that fact but I think it all lands better if I just spill it all out at the end while I'm having the revelations like this. Given the utter absurdities of this modern era where we live in Clown World, I think it only makes sense that it would boil down to something like that.

Honestly I think it's even more absurd that it took a proc of a proc of a bot saying things for me to figure out what was wrong with myself.

I feel like I've just torn out a chunk of my soul and rended it unto the canvas for this. I don't really know why this helped me, but I hope this helps you too. Stay fresh out there, and if you're going to also venture forth to that millennial retirement home of a launch, maybe I'll see you in Azeroth in early November for World of Warcraft Forever. I'm gonna go in blind, you should too. We'll figure it all out together, one terrible loot table at a time.
